items.prompt: Define urbanisation.
items.canonical_answer: Urbanisation is an increase in the proportion of a population living in urban areas; distinguish it from an increase in urban population alone.
marking_guidance: Meaning: increase in the proportion living in urban areas, not merely the urban number.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Describe the urbanisation pattern in this original fictional country: period 1 urban 400,000 of total 1,000,000; period 2 urban 600,000 of total 2,000,000.
items.canonical_answer: The urban population increases by 200,000 but its share falls from 40% to 30%. Thus the larger number does not show urbanisation during the interval; the share falls by 10 percentage points.
marking_guidance: Evidence: use the urban counts and total-population denominators.
Relationship: contrast rising numbers with the falling share.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Calculate the urban population share in a fictional country with 360,000 urban residents among 900,000 total. Show working.
items.canonical_answer: 360,000 ÷ 900,000 = 0.4; multiplying by 100 gives 40% of the population.
marking_guidance: Working: urban divided by total, converted to a percentage.
Unit: percent of the population.

items.prompt: Explain the error in saying urbanisation must have occurred because an invented country’s urban population rose from 400,000 to 600,000 while its total rose from one million to two million.
items.canonical_answer: The urban number rises but its share falls from 40% to 30%. Urbanisation requires a rising proportion, so test the urban count against the total population in each period rather than the count alone.
marking_guidance: Error: urban population growth is substituted for urbanisation.
Distinction: number versus rising share, supported by the denominators.

items.prompt: Explain how rural–urban migration can contribute to urbanisation.
items.canonical_answer: If net movement adds to the urban population relative to the rural population, the urban share can rise. Other population changes and definitions also matter, so migration is a contributor rather than the definition.
marking_guidance: Reason: connect net movement to the relative share, rather than equating any migration with urbanisation.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Describe the relationship in this original fictional comparison: A’s urban share rises from 30% to 45% with annual net rural–urban inflow 5,000; B’s rises from 70% to 72% with inflow 500. Comparable periods and definitions are used.
items.canonical_answer: A combines a larger inflow with a larger share increase: 15 percentage points compared with two in B. B starts more urban but urbanises more slowly by this share measure.
marking_guidance: Evidence: compare both inflow and the changes in share.
Relationship: distinguish starting level and rate of urbanisation; causation is not established by the pair alone.

items.prompt: Describe two broad characteristics that can occur in industrialised-country urban patterns.
items.canonical_answer: A high existing urban share can reflect earlier industrial and service concentration. Later movement between urban areas or towards suburbs can change city populations without necessarily increasing the national urban share.
marking_guidance: Feature: two relevant qualified characteristics, not a claim that every country follows the same path.

items.prompt: Describe two possible characteristics of rapid urban growth in a developing economy.

items.prompt: Explain the sanitation problem in an invented settlement where household numbers rise but toilets and waste-removal capacity stay unchanged and overflows are recorded.

Consequence: connect the recorded overflow to waste containment, without inventing disease statistics.

items.prompt: Explain which option to phase first in a fictional housing programme. Upgrading water in the present settlement reaches 200 households quickly but leaves crowded plots. A funded serviced extension can house 350 households with a work-bus connection, but takes two years. Both are feasible and funds cannot complete both immediately.
items.canonical_answer: The existing-area upgrade tackles current water need sooner, benefiting residents who already live there. The extension offers more space and wider coverage, with a credible work link, but leaves an access delay. Immediate upgrading is preferable where present water need is urgent, while reserving a staged extension for crowding. If safe interim water is already assured, the larger extension may deserve priority. Time, reach and livelihood access all matter.
marking_guidance: Judgement: compare genuine benefits and costs against the stated aim.
Reason: develop each option using supplied evidence, weigh the trade-off, and give a conditional conclusion.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Explain which serviced-site option better fits a fictional low-income community. Both sites have water and usable work-bus connections. A is near jobs with higher plot payments; B has lower plot payments but longer journeys and higher travel costs. The budget evidence does not show which total cost households can afford.
items.canonical_answer: A reduces travel time and costs, but its plot payments may exclude some households. B lowers the entry cost but adds recurring travel expense and time. Compare combined housing and travel costs with household resources before declaring either affordable. A is stronger where the payment schedule is manageable; B may suit households prioritising lower upfront cost if the journey remains affordable. A cheap plot price alone cannot settle practical access.
marking_guidance: Judgement: compare genuine benefits and costs against the stated aim.
Reason: develop each option using supplied evidence, weigh the trade-off, and give a conditional conclusion.

items.prompt: Explain whether a fictional new town is suitable for relocation. It offers serviced homes and funded transport to jobs but a 50-minute journey. Upgrading the present area keeps a 15-minute journey but leaves less space and takes disruptive building work. Both have feasible finance. The aim is housing and livelihood improvement.
items.canonical_answer: The town offers better space and services with a credible employment link, but the longer journey adds time and may weaken household routines. Upgrading preserves nearby work and social links, while its crowding and disruption remain costs. Prefer upgrading where livelihood proximity is most valuable and adequate improvement is possible; choose relocation where space and services outweigh the journey burden for participating households. Consultation and combined access costs should inform the judgement.
marking_guidance: Judgement: compare genuine benefits and costs against the stated aim.
Reason: develop each option using supplied evidence, weigh the trade-off, and give a conditional conclusion.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Differentiate between classifying a person’s employment status and classifying an activity as formal or informal.
items.canonical_answer: Employment status concerns whether or how fully the person has work; formal or informal classification concerns the activity’s registration or regulatory arrangements. Either type of activity can provide employment.

items.prompt: Describe the work pattern in an original fictional survey of 100 people available for work: 30 have no job and are seeking work; 40 have jobs but work fewer paid hours than they want and are available for; 30 have jobs with their desired hours.
items.canonical_answer: Thirty people are unemployed. Forty are employed but underemployed in hours. Thirty are employed with their desired hours. Thus 70 have a job (40 + 30), while a different overlapping total of 70 have unmet work needs (30 + 40). These totals describe different characteristics, not two separate groups of 70.
marking_guidance: Evidence: distinguish all three categories and reconcile 30 + 40 + 30 = 100.
Relationship: explain why some employment and unmet work needs can overlap.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: State (a) the difference between urbanisation and urban population growth [2]. Explain (b) the service implication in an invented town where households rise from 600 to 1,000 while functioning shared water points remain at four, with unchanged supply per point [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) Urbanisation is a rise in the urban population share, while urban population growth is an increase in the number living in urban areas. (b) Households per point rise from 150 to 250. With unchanged supply at each point, demand pressure rises and practical collection access may worsen unless capacity or demand arrangements change. This is evidence of service pressure, not a measured queue time or proof of the national urbanisation rate.
marking_guidance: Point (a), 2 marks: number versus proportion distinction.
Development (b), up to 4 marks: combine household growth and fixed supply capacity, derive the pressure and explain the bounded access effect.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.

items.prompt: Calculate (a) the urban population share in fictional Country A with 450,000 urban residents among 900,000 total, showing working [2]. Explain (b) whether the country with the higher share should automatically receive more urban water support: B has urban share 70% and safe-water access among urban households 90%; A has access 50%. The aim is to identify unmet urban water needs [4].
items.canonical_answer: (a) 450,000 ÷ 900,000 = 0.5; multiplying by 100 gives 50%. (b) No. B’s larger urban share does not show a larger access gap: 10% of its urban households lack safe-water access compared with 50% in A. A warrants priority investigation for the stated access aim. Household counts, locations and costs are still needed for final allocation, so proportions alone do not establish the number needing support.
marking_guidance: Evidence (a), 2 marks: correct urban/total calculation and 50%.
Meaning (b), up to 4 marks: distinguish urban share from the access gap, use both access figures and justify a bounded investigation decision rather than inventing household numbers.
Original indicative practice guidance; not an official mark scheme.
